https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Isabelle Rose Welsh was the victim of a ‘sadistic’ campaign of abuse, the judge said. Photograph: Cleveland police/PA View image in fullscreen Isabelle Rose Welsh was the victim of a ‘sadistic’ campaign of abuse, the judge said. Photograph: Cleveland police/PA Police Cleveland police failed to arrest man who later killed two-year-old girl Harrison Simpson was subject of arrest warrant for breach of court order 18 months before killing girlfriend’s daughter Neha Gohil and PA Media Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.47 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 13.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Cleveland police failed to arrest a paedophile for breaching a non-molestation order, 18 months before he sexually assaulted and murdered and his girlfriend’s two-year-old daughter, a court heard. Isabelle Welsh died on 14 September 2025 after what police described as a “campaign of violence” against her. The two-year-old collapsed at her home in Teesside after weeks of abuse that left her covered in bruises and with 21 broken bones. The toddler’s mother, Alexandra Walker, 26, and Walker’s boyfriend, Harrison Simpson, 22, were convicted of murder and child cruelty on Thursday after a trial at Teesside crown court. View image in fullscreen Alexandra Walker and Harrison Simpson. Photograph: Cleveland police/PA Simpson was also convicted of sexually assaulting Isabelle before her death. Walker was cleared of that charge. The pair were jailed for life, with minimum terms of 28 years and six months for Simpson and 22 years for Walker, both minus time spent on remand. Cleveland police admitted that officers failed to execute a warrant issued by Teesside magistrates court for Simpson’s arrest in March 2024, according to the Sunday Times. Simpson had failed to attend court for breaching a non-molestation order, which is an injunction designed to protect victims of domestic abuse, when the warrant was issued in March 2024. It is understood the non-molestation order was in place after reports Simpson had harassed and threatened a woman. Cleveland police said in a statement: “Multiple inquiries and arrest attempts were carried out to try to locate and arrest him, but these proved unsuccessful.” It added: “We recognise the time Simpson had an outstanding arrest warrant is far from adequate. A review of this was immediately conducted upon his arrest for murder. “This review, along with a determination to continually improve our processes around suspect management, has led to a number of recent changes, such as ongoing improved visibility across the force around outstanding warrants, a comprehensive data system which tracks all outstanding warrants, and stringent oversight including a governance group led by a superintendent.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion At the sentencing, Justice Norton said Isabelle’s murder was “distressing” and said the two-year-old had endured a “sadistic” campaign of abuse. “Any death is a tragedy. The death of a very young child at the hands of those who should have cared for, protected, and loved her – as she no doubt loved them – is particularly distressing for all involved,” the judge said. A statement by the family of Isabelle Welsh previously said: “Isabelle should have had her whole life ahead of her, but she was taken from us in the most heartbreaking way. She was so loved and our lives will never be the same without her.” The senior investigating officer Det Ch Insp Steve Chatterton said the case was one of the worst he had dealt with. “The pain and suffering she experienced at the hands of Walker and Simpson was sickening,” he said. https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/articl.text: “Miluim [IDF reserve duty] is like being on an emotional roller coaster,” was how Esther described the last few years of her husband being at war. “A rollercoaster that you forget that you're on, but you wake up right before the drop and try to breathe through it and not vomit.”Esther, 36, was born in New York but moved to Israel in 2005, aged 15, as part of an immersive high school program called Naale. Following this, she did two years of national service in the Gaza border area, and then began a degree in glass and ceramic design at Bezalel QAcademy of Arts and Design in Jerusalem. While working at Artza, the company of Itai, the brother of Jerusalem Post photojournalist Chen Schimmel, she met her husband Yonah, who is Itai's friend.Esther and Yonah began their life in Tel Aviv and were 26 weeks pregnant with their first daughter, Hallel, when war broke out on October 7.“There was a siren, and we jumped out of bed and went into the hallway. But we had no reason to think that it was a big deal, and my husband said he was going to get ready to go to the synagogue,” she said.As he was getting ready, his phone rang. The two knew immediately that it was the army, as no one else would call on Shabbat.“He said, 'I'm getting called in.' And I told him, 'Absolutely not. Do not answer your phone. If it's that important, they'll reach you after Shabbat.'”Yonah left for synagogue. While he was on his way back, there was a second siren, and Esther headed to the shelter alone.“I remember thinking that that was the moment I became a mom. Even though I hadn't given birth.”October 7 felt differentEsther told the Post that she had lived through previous wars in Israel, but October 7 felt different. “I was shaking. I didn't know what happened in the South, but I was terrified for my baby. I was reacting in a way that I'd never experienced.”When Yonah returned from synagogue, he answered a second call from his reserve unit. It was only then that Esther learned Hamas had infiltrated southern Israel.“Yonah told me that Hamas had broken into Israel, that they infiltrated the South. At that point, we had just heard that about 70 people had been killed. We heard about Nova [Supernova music festival massacre]. We didn't know yet that they [terrorists] were in the kibbutzim. I just broke down crying. I was sobbing hysterically, I couldn't breathe, I was so terrified for him.”Once she collected herself, Esther asked her husband a question that shocked him: “Do you have a will?”“I told him, if something happens, I don't care about our stuff. I need to know what happens to me. If something happens to you and they can't find your body, how long do I have to wait before I'm considered not married anymore? I do not want to be an agunah.”“He replied: 'I cannot wrap my head around that. We're not discussing this. I'm alive, I'm fine.'”Feelings of anxiety and guiltOn Saturday evening, Yonah was called up to serve with his unit: 551 [the elite paratrooper reservist unit]. Esther left to stay with her in-laws in order not to be alone.“I was just having anxiety attack after anxiety attack; it was constant. At some point, Yonah called me and said, 'I need to have a real conversation with you. I understand that it's really scary for you and that you have no control over your hormones, and it's a wild situation that you're pregnant and I'm here. But I need you to be my rock. I need to be able to talk to you about what I'm going through and where I'm going. So you need to figure out what you need to do in order to become my support system because that's what I need right now in order to survive.'”Esther said she felt guilty.“My initial reaction was that I felt selfish because he was going through something so much more scary and existential. He was going to be physically going into one of the most dangerous war zones in the world.”Fears started to run through her head: What if Yonah never got to meet their baby? What if she had to give birth in a bomb shelter, alone, without him?Around this time, Esther's aunt in the US called and suggested she come to stay with her and recuperate. While Esther immediately refused to abandon her husband, Yonah felt differently: “He said, 'Whatever you need to do, you have to do because I need you mentally stable.'”A friend helped Esther secure a seat on an evacuation flight to Poland, from where she flew to her aunt in Florida for several weeks until she felt able to return home.“We had gone through Operation Protective Edge [in 2014], so when Yonah told me he was going to Gaza, I figured he would be home in 10-14 days. I knew I had to be home when he came home for the first time.”On returning to Israel, Esther started volunteering. One day, she got a message on her phone from an unknown number. Yonah had written her a letter inside Gaza, and someone had driven it out into Israel, taken a picture, and a commander had texted it to her.“It was like 21st-century snail mail. I had to physically write a response, send it to them, and then they printed it and took it to Yonah.”A few days later, Yonah came out of Gaza and the two reunited for the first time in a month.“This was the start of nearly three years of him going in and out,” she recalled.In late December 2023, one of the men from Yonah's unit was killed, and another one was severely injured, and this led to the unit being released from reserves at the start of January.At this point, for the first time since October 7, the two were back in their apartment in Tel Aviv, which Esther said was “surreal.” After three months of seeing each other for a day here, a day there, they were suddenly living together again.An overloaded hospital and a traumatic birthAt 35 weeks pregnant, Esther began having contractions, which ultimately persisted for three weeks. At 4 a.m. one morning, when she was 38 weeks pregnant, she went into labor.When the couple arrived at Ichilov Hospital, they were met with an overloaded maternity unit, as the hospital had absorbed all the patients evacuated from the North and South.“I was told that there were women who were more urgent, and that I was not far enough along to get a bed.'”“It was pouring rain. I actively labored for 15 hours, eight of which I was standing at the front of the hospital.”Esther stopped relaying her birth story at this point because of the extreme trauma of what happened next.What followed was a six-month recovery. She couldn't be alone with her baby until Hallel was four months old because she physically could not hold her. Esther ended up having reparative surgery two months after Hallel was born.Having moved to Ra'anana after the birth, Esther thankfully had the help of her in-laws, who, to this day, have been above-and-beyond in the way they have shown up, she said. “It was the most responsible decision we've ever made. We wanted to stay in Tel Aviv, but our reality just didn't allow for it.”Because she was so incapacitated during this time, Yonah took over a large amount of what new mothers do, and as a result, Hallel became extremely bonded to her father, something that remains today.Yonah's next round of reserve duty was when Hallel was five months old.At that point, Esther was more capable but “still not 100%” and had someone coming and helping her every day. Yonah agreed to go for half of the time he was called up for, doing one and a half months instead of three.“We tried to video call Yonah, and Hallel couldn't understand the concept that she couldn't reach him through the computer. I have never seen her scream like that; she was terrified, she couldn't process why she couldn't touch him.”They did not attempt a video call again.Twenty-one months after Hallel was born, Esther gave birth to their second baby, Mia.While she was pregnant with Mia, the first Iran war broke out. Esther said that was the first time she began to see miluim in a negative light.“I was seven months pregnant running to the mamad [safe room] with a one and a half year old while Yonah was called in. Until this point, I understood miluim, but suddenly it felt pointless. I needed him more at home than the army did on the Jordanian border.”Thankfully, the second birth experience was “incredible” and not in any way comparable to the first. Yonah was home, having just finished another round of two months in the army.Motherhood in a time of war, with a husband fighting, is no walk in the park. Esther said that the two have survived it by “making a game plan” and being practical.“For me, as the mother, it's been about trying to find things that would help me through those really tough moments. You have to enter into this superhuman space; people don't see the small, tiny things that happen day to day, which actually take an exceedingly huge amount of internal resources and power.”Additionally, she said that there's a societal expectation that wives and partners of men in miluim be okay because they must be used to it. “There is an expectation that you have to be this strong home front, and that you shouldn't complain about it. There used to be more sympathy, but it's not like what it used to be.“It's not that people don't care. It's that they just want life to be normal again, which I completely understand. This has been going on for such a long time already. It's uncomfortable to think about war, and that there are families for whom life is just not normal on a regular basis.”Just because people like her don't ask for help as much anymore doesn't mean they don't need it, she said.“If you know someone who's going through it, just check in and get a cup of coffee with them. To just be there for these people is huge.”The need to not be alone, to have a distraction, is especially true for Esther in the moments right before Yonah leaves. She spoke of the process of being photographed by the Post for “HER,” which happened to be on the day of Yonah going to miluim.“You can see it in the pictures. I can't stop crying. And then there's the picture where Yonah is walking out the door, and I'm holding Hallel and my eyes are half closed. That's me gathering myself. I cry, get it out of my system, and then I'm done.”After he walked out the door, the family had a little dance party.“I guess part of our distraction, part of our survival kit, is putting on music and having a dance.”Esther said that if she had to sum up having a husband in miluim, she would compare it to being on a roller coaster.“When you're on a roller coaster, there's the climb, and then there's the crazy part, and then there's the plateau. There's the climb to the miluim, and then there's the drop of him leaving, and then the crazy twists and turns when we are figuring out how we navigate this: How do we breathe through this? And then it's over, and we can breathe. And then it happens all over again.”What helps them through the twists and turns?“We find a rhythm. I think it comes down to communication - really good communication. We get really frustrated with each other, but we try to talk about it as much as possible.”However, she said, sometimes these important conversations get cut short.“He leaves while we're working through an issue, and we have to continue it via whatever limited communication we have this time or wait until he's home again.”There's also a palpable tension in the air when he's gone, she added.“I think it's the weight of his absence and fear that he's not coming back. It's just a big rip in our equilibrium when he's gone.”During the time Yonah is away, Esther said, she has to function for the girls, but the fear is constantly hanging over her. Often, her imagination has gotten the best of her, and more than once she found herself thinking sounds in the hallway were someone from the army coming to knock on the door and tell her of her husband's death.Hallel is now old enough to understand that he leaves again and again but not why. In the beginning, it didn't seem to affect her, but as time has passed, she has become more and more clingy, throws tantrums, and gets upset. Now that Yonah is home, Hallel constantly checks in on where he is.“I've caught her walking around saying, 'Abba is home. He's just working.'”All this being said, Esther spoke glowingly about her husband. “He's just a very empathetic, kind person,” she said, adding that he is “100% committed to being her partner and the best father he can be.”“He's done the work and is very in tune with himself and knows what he is capable of giving to his family, to miluim, to his work. I love that he is connected to himself in that way.”Looking back, Esther said, she is proud of herself.“I am most proud of the fact that I had two kids in this crazy, insane time. I went back for a second. I'm really proud of myself for going through the process – I think it was the bravest thing I've ever done.”

https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-v.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen cautioned against cuts to the EU’s next seven-year budget in a rebuke to Germany's calls to dramatically slash spending. During a speech in the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday, von der Leyen said that reducing the size of the EU’s common cash pot would undermine critical EU-wide priorities such as competitiveness and energy autonomy. “I would like to caution against large cuts. It would risk cutting deep into critical priorities that we all together have agreed on,” von der Leyen told MEPs. Advertisement Advertisement The warning comes days before the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the budget talks, is expected to put forward a budget negotiating document with new figures. Von der Leyen had previously hailed the Commission's budget proposal for 2028-2034 as “the most ambitious ever proposed.” But Tuesday, as negotiations among governments enter crunch time, she struck a more cautious note. In a message to Berlin, von der Leyen recalled that the Commission’s budget proposal represents 1.26% of the European Union’s gross national income — a relatively small increase from the current seven-year cash pot. She also underscored the need to approve “a significant package of new own resources,” which are EU-wide taxes to finance the budget and reduce national contributions to Brussels. The bloc’s governments are racing to reach an agreement by the end of the year, before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to disrupt the negotiations. Despite the looming deadline, EU leaders are still far apart over the size of the new budget. Advertisement Advertisement Germany and its allies in Northern Europe have pressured Dublin to make cuts worth hundreds of billions of euros across the board. But 17 EU countries from Southern and Eastern Europe — led by Italy and Romania — are pushing in the opposite direction. They asked to preserve farmers’ subsidies and regional payouts, known as cohesion policy, in a joint letter last week. During a separate speech to the European Parliament on Tuesday, Portuguese Prime Minister Luís Montenegro said that “there is no European competitiveness without cohesion, and no European cohesion without competitiveness.” In a rebuke to the frugals, Montenegro said that Portugal’s contribution to the EU budget as a share of its gross domestic product is higher than that of Germany and other wealthier countries. “Giving 10 out of 100 is much more than giving 50 out of 1,000," he told MEPs. But Germany insists that its budget contributions are too high. In a thinly veiled threat on Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that “having no new financial framework is by far the most financially advantageous solution for Germany.” Advertisement Advertisement However, he added that such a scenario would restrict the EU’s ability to act and renewed calls to end the negotiations by the end of the year. Several European officials believe that Dublin will propose budget cuts exceeding €100 billion. The proposal is expected to be put forward Saturday and be discussed by EU ambassadors Sunday. This article has been updated.

https://thesun.ng/wright-urges-premier-l.text: Tinubu, Lawal get student backing as Zamfara unveils 2027 Campus Ambassadors 30 September 2026 3:56 am WAT By The Sun Follow Us on Google The JAGABA/DAUDA Students’ Mandate 2027, Zamfara State Chapter, has launched its Campus Ambassadors initiative, pledging to mobilise students across tertiary institutions in the state for the re-election of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and Governor Dauda Lawal in the 2027 elections. The group said its mobilisation campaign would focus on engaging students, organising campus discussions and highlighting education programmes and interventions attributed to the federal and Zamfara State governments. Speaking at the launch, the Convener, Comrade Bilyaminu Badarawa, described the initiative as a strategic platform for reaching Zamfara’s student population and drawing attention to developments in the education sector. He emphasised that the mandate is rooted in what the group described as tangible and verifiable achievements in the education sector that have directly impacted Nigerian students and the people of Zamfara State. Badarawa said: “We are here to launch a movement that will engage students with the developments taking place in the education sector. Our Campus Ambassadors will take this message to campuses across Zamfara, engage their fellow students and ensure that young people are properly informed about the programmes and interventions affecting their education and future.” The group cited the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) student-loan scheme as one of the major education initiatives of the Tinubu administration. NELFUND reported in August 2026 that more than 1.6 million student-loan applications had been processed, with over N322 billion disbursed. It also highlighted investments in technical and vocational education and training, research, infrastructure and institutional support, as well as the federal government’s efforts to address disruptions in tertiary education. He added, “The administration successfully reached a comprehensive agreement with ASUU, ending a crisis that had lingered for 16 years and leading to improved salaries, allowances, pensions, research funding and working conditions for university staff. TETFund Infrastructure Projects: Massive infrastructure development across higher institutions nationwide. “Research and Innovation Grants: Billions of naira in grants awarded for research projects in tertiary institutions, covering health, agriculture, clean energy and defence technology. “Institutional Support in Zamfara: Support for Federal University Gusau and the Federal University of Health Sciences, Tsafe. UBEC Smart Model School: Zamfara is among the states covered by the Federal Government’s UBEC Smart Model School programme. “UBEC Funding for Basic Education: Zamfara is covered by the federal Universal Basic Education intervention framework, through which states can access federal matching-grant funding for basic education, including infrastructure, instructional materials and teacher development. “ In November 2023, Governor Lawal declared a state of emergency in the education sector, making education one of the administration’s major priorities. Renovation and Reconstruction of More Than 500 Schools: The state government reports that more than 500 public schools have been reconstructed, renovated and equipped across Zamfara. “The government reported providing more than 12,000 two-seater desks for pupils and students, alongside hundreds of teachers’ tables and chairs. Recruitment of 2,000 Teachers: In January 2025, Governor Lawal approved the recruitment of 2,000 qualified teachers, with initial emphasis on Mathematics, English, Chemistry, Physics, Biology, ICT and Entrepreneurship. “Payment of Outstanding WAEC and NECO Debts: The administration paid outstanding examination debts inherited from previous administrations, including ₦1.4 billion to WAEC and ₦320.7 million to NECO. Release of Previously Withheld Examination Results: Students whose WAEC and NECO results had been withheld because of unpaid fees were able to access their results after the government settled outstanding obligations. “The state also paid for the 2024 WAEC examination, allowing public-school students to participate. 408,137 Teaching and Learning Materials: In September 2025, the government announced the distribution of 408,137 teaching and learning materials to public schools. UBEC additionally provided 77,609 materials, while UNICEF supplied 5,000 climate-change and education early-warning handbooks. “School Feeding Programme: The administration launched a school-feeding initiative aimed at improving school enrolment and retention while addressing hunger and malnutrition among pupils. Partnerships with NGOs supported feeding programmes in several LGAs. “Support for Students Whose University Certificates Were Withheld: In January 2026, the government settled outstanding tuition fees for 50 Zamfara students of Crescent University, Abeokuta, enabling them to receive certificates that had reportedly been withheld for nine years. “Reform of State-Owned Tertiary Institutions: In January 2025, governing councils and boards were inaugurated for six state-owned tertiary institutions, including Zamfara State University, Abdu Gusau Polytechnic, College of Education Maru, College of Nursing and Midwifery Gusau, College of Health Sciences and Technology Tsafe, and College of Agriculture and Animal Science Bakura. Education Governance and Quality-Assurance Reforms: “In July 2026, Governor Lawal signed Executive Orders covering education financing, school protection, quality assurance, school health, security, unified examinations, inclusive education, STEM, TVET and digital education. The national curriculum was also distributed to public schools. “120-Day Rapid Education Intervention Plan: In April 2026, the State Executive Council approved a 120-day plan covering school mapping, infrastructure assessment, payroll audits, teacher development, digital transformation and student welfare. It also approved work towards a unified Education Sector Bill covering education from ECCDE through tertiary level. “Improved Institutional Support for Higher Education: In September 2026, official vehicles were distributed to several higher-education institutions and education agencies, including Federal University Gusau, Zamfara State University, Abdu Gusau Polytechnic, College of Nursing and Midwifery, the Teachers Service Board and Quality Assurance bodies. “Scholarship and Student Support: At the Federal University Gusau convocation in 2024, the governor announced a state scholarship for the university’s overall best graduating student. The state’s 2025 budget-performance report also records a domestic scholarship scheme. “The newly inaugurated Campus Ambassadors were charged with the responsibility of grassroots mobilisation, voter education and engaging students on education-related programmes and developments at both federal and state levels. “We cannot afford to return to a past where examination results were withheld, teachers were unpaid and classrooms collapsed. The JAGABA/DAUDA STUDENTS’ MANDATE 2027 is committed to ensuring that the voices of Zamfara students are heard and their interests protected,” the Convener stated. “The future of Zamfara depends significantly on the quality of education available to its young people. Our responsibility as students and young citizens is to understand what is being done, engage constructively and make our voices heard. The JAGABA/DAUDA STUDENTS’ MANDATE 2027 is committed to ensuring that the interests and aspirations of Zamfara students remain at the centre of our mobilisation,” he added. The event concluded with a call for students across Zamfara State to support the Tinubu and Lawal ticket in the 2027 elections, with the newly inaugurated Campus Ambassadors pledging to mobilise students and young people across tertiary institutions in the state.
